sentences.text: Lusotitan was a massive, plant-eating sauropod that lived in Portugal during the Late Jurassic period.
This giant creature grew to a length of 21 meters and had a body mass ranging from 25 to 30 tonnes.
Its anatomy featured long forearms, with the upper arm bone measuring 2.05 meters and the thigh bone reaching 2 meters.
A large sternal plate preserved in the fossil record suggests the animal may have exceeded its standard size estimates.
It stands as the largest dinosaur species identified within the Lourinhã Formation area.
Manuel de Matos first uncovered large sauropod fossils in the Lourinhã Formation in 1947.
Albert-Félix de Lapparent and Georges Zbyszewski originally named the species Brachiosaurus atalaiensis in 1957.
Researchers Octávio Mateus and Miguel Telles Antunes later established the separate genus Lusotitan in 2003.
The known remains consist of a partial skeleton that lacks a skull and includes vertebrae found in multiple locations.
The collection includes 28 vertebrae along with various elements of the appendicular skeleton.
These fossils were found in the Sobral unit of the Lourinhã Formation, near Atalaia in the municipality of Peralta, Estremadura, Portugal.
Due to similarities with Brachiosaurus, Lusotitan was originally placed within the Brachiosauridae family.
Later phylogenetic analyses placed Lusotitan as a sister taxon to Titanosauriformes at the base of Macronaria, alongside other Eurasian sauropods like Dongbeititan, Galvesaurus, and Aragosaurus.
In 2019, Mannion and colleagues re-included Lusotitan in the original Brachiosauridae family.
Lusotitan lived in the Lourinhã Formation of western Portugal during the Kimmeridgian or Tithonian ages of the Late Jurassic.
The animal lived between 152.21 and 145.06 million years ago, spanning the Kimmeridgian to Tithonian stages.

It coexisted with predatory theropods like Allosaurus and Torvosaurus, the ankylosaurian Dracopelta, other sauropods such as Bothriospondylus and Lourinhasaurus, and stegosaurs including Dacentrurus and Miragaia.
It is debated whether Galvesaurus or Galveosaurus are junior synonyms of Lusotitan; while some researchers suggested synonymy in 2017, a 2019 study found distinct characters making them sister taxa.
